newsitem.title: ISRAEL: FEATURE - Ancient Jewish secrets unravel at Israeli show.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Ancient Jewish secrets unravel at Israeli show.

text.p: Tuvia bin Eli bin Khalaf had such a rotten reputation that his prospective wife Faiza refused to marry him unless he stopped his foolish antics.

"I will associate with proper men and not corrupt men. I will not bring into my house licentious men, buffoons, frivolous jesters and good-for-nothings," he pledged in a pre-nuptial agreement in 1047.
"I will not purchase for myself a slave girl as long as this Faiza is with me in marriage, except with her explicit consent."
Tuvia and Faiza's agreement is a part of 140,000 scraps of paper detailing mediaeval Jewish life discovered by accident a century ago in a Cairo genizah, a storage place for old religious documents.
"The only thing that's anywhere near it (in importance) is the Dead Sea Scrolls," said Dr Stefan Reif, director of Genizah Research at the Cambridge University Library which owns the fragments.
Found in the ancient Ben Ezra synagogue in the Egyptian capital, the genizah scraps have vanished and reappeared several times and once escaped being burned as rubbish.
Researchers finally sorted out the fragments, analysed half of them, and loaned a record 50 choice items to the Israel museum for a display that runs until October.
GENIZAH CLEARS UP QUESTIONS OF JEWISH CULTURE
A future display on such a scale is unlikely because the scraps, although kept in protective plastic, are fragile.
"There are gaps in Jewish culture that are cleared up in the genizah," Reif said.

Jews debated for centuries whether the scholar Ben Sira's book of Jewish proverbs was first written in Hebrew as no old Hebrew version could be found. Among the documents found in the genizah was a 10th century Hebrew version.

The fragments also include a text detailing the religious beliefs of a Jewish sect, crushed by the Romans in A.D. 68, whose literature reappeared in the Dead Sea Scrolls found at Qumran in the West Bank 50 years ago.
"(This shows) all these people did not die, they were not all killed. The Dead Sea sect, the Qumran sect, did not effectively disappear. Many of their ideas, their texts, lived on," Reif said.

What astounded researchers was that a quarter of the 10th to 13th century documents written in Hebrew, Aramaic and Judeo-Arabic deal with purely secular life. No other genizah has been found to contain such documents.
"For some reason unknown to us, the Cairo genizah got documents of all different kinds," Reif said. "Perhaps it was (because of) Jewish respect for the written word."

In addition to famous religious tracts, it is these scraps -- the deeds, wills and letters and marriage and divorce contracts -- that exhibition curator Daisy Raccah-Djivre chose to display prominently.
GLOOMY HISTORY SURROUNDS THE SCRAPS

"You can read about how the schoolteacher sends a note to the parents, and the parents ask for more notes so the child will become afraid and learn more. Sometimes I can hardly believe these are the contents," she said.
But a gloomy history surrounds the scraps. The first two genizah scholars died early deaths, and 100,000 of the fragments sat for years in dusty crates, wasting away, before they were rediscovered.
"Whoever touched the genizah, horrible things happened to them," said Reif, referring to the scholars without elaborating. He has worked with the scraps for 25 years without incident.

About 70,000 similar fragments turned up later in the nearby Bassatin cemetery and several synagogues in the old city of Fustat where the Jewish community thrived in the mediaeval era. Mystery surrounds them too.

Fustat was destroyed by fire in the 12th century and has been neglected ever since. A garbage dump now encroaches its ruins. The tombs, where Reif says more documents may still be buried, are now inhabited by Cairo's poor in what local residents call the City of the Dead.
Although Cairo's dry climate helped preserve the scraps for centuries, future discoveries could prove difficult.
"People live in the tombs," Reif said. "There are fragments there and people live there."
